idiom_name: compile-time registration into a registry (plugin.Open only where unavoidable)
alternative: Compose components at compile time: interface implementations registered at init() time (or selected by a constructor) from configuration - keeping static binaries, type safety and normal test coverage. Where genuine run-time extension is required, move the component out of process (subprocess over RPC/gRPC, or a WASM host such as wazero), so 'unlink' becomes process or module termination.
implementation_notes: Go's plugin package is the only built-in route to loading code at run time, and it is explicitly unsuitable for this pattern: plugins are supported only on Linux, FreeBSD and macOS, host and plugin must be built with exactly the same toolchain, build tags, flags and dependency versions, and the documentation states that 'A plugin is only initialized once, and cannot be closed' - the unlink half of Component Configurator is impossible and hot reconfiguration degenerates into process restarts. The Go-idiomatic substitute is configuration over compile-time composition: components are interfaces registered at init() time into a registry (or provided by a constructor that main selects from configuration), which keeps static binaries and full test coverage. When runtime extensibility is genuinely required, put the component out of process so that replacing it is a process/worker restart, not a code unload.
pitfalls: plugin.Open() is unavailable on Windows and requires plugin and host to be built with exactly the same toolchain, build tags, flags and dependency versions; a mismatch surfaces at load time in production, not at build time.
Plugins cannot be closed: every open maps code for the life of the process, so 'reload a component' can only mean restart the process (or run it in its own process).

Interface identity across a plugin boundary depends on identical package paths and module versions - a plugin built against a different version of the shared contract yields a type that does not satisfy the host interface and fails only at the assertion.
